trigger: Maxwell, after XDR-preset test also failed: 'still getting the negative space lines in the shadows' -- light lines where shadow is missing, not dark bands.

task1_corpus_reread.method: Read the FULL row-mean luminance profile (not just the rows the old dark-dip detector had already flagged) for the prior session's confirmed-banded frames, and for the confirmed-clean control moving_8.
task1_corpus_reread.finding: moving_1 and moving_6 (both confirmed TRUE bands in the prior session) show an ALTERNATING pattern: baseline ~20-30, thin DARK dips to ~7-10 (what the old dark-only classifier caught) immediately paired with thin LIGHT PEAKS up to ~55-75 a few rows away. The light peaks are the LARGER-magnitude anomaly: moving_1 peak delta ~+35 to +40 vs the dip's ~-13 to -18; moving_6 peak delta ~+30 to +49 vs the dip's ~-16 to -22. moving_8 (confirmed clean, same row range) shows neither -- a smooth 25-31 band, no swings either direction.
task1_corpus_reread.verdict: YES -- the historical hits were genuinely bidirectional (light AND dark), and the light component is the dominant one. The old classifier partially detected this phenomenon via its darker, smaller-magnitude side effect, never via its actual larger-magnitude light-peak signature. This does NOT mean all 2800 prior null frames were on the wrong track for having zero dark hits -- it means a light-only or light+dark classifier is required to know whether they truly had zero artifact-related activity.

task2_classifier.design: classify_light_seam.py: same 2-stage design as classify_burst.py (full-width per-frame detector + same-scale world-coordinate persistence check across the capture burst), polarity flipped to detect a row run BRIGHTER than its local vertical baseline by >=10 luminance levels across >=85% of row width.
task2_classifier.calibration_validation: 3/3 true positives (moving_1, moving_2, moving_6) correctly flagged, 0% false-negative rate on confirmed positives. 1/18 false positive (preseat_0, the SAME understood whole-map/low-zoom-grid blind spot as the dark-dip classifier -- does not apply to the deployed zoomed-follow-camera experiments). Identical error profile to the validated dark-dip classifier.
task2_classifier.synthetic_injection_validation: Injected a synthetic 2px-tall, full-width brightness step into a known-clean dark frame (seated_rest_0) at increasing deltas. Reliable detection at delta>=10 luminance levels; not detected below that -- matches the classifier's own per_pixel_peak=8/peak_thresh=10 parameters, giving a concrete, quantified sensitivity floor rather than an assumed one.

task3_mechanism.code_path: src/ctf/global.nim proc addFogRuns (~line 3989): fog-of-war is NOT one shape -- it is MANY separate 'run' objects, one per horizontal stretch of unseen cells per row of the visibility grid (FovGridW x FovGridH, FovCellSize=8px cells), rebuilt from scratch every tick from sim.playerFov(playerIndex).visible. Each run gets its own objectId (FogObjectBase + runIndex) and is placed via addBoardObject at an INTEGER cell-aligned position (run.cx*FovCellSize, run.cy*FovCellSize).
task3_mechanism.client_path: client/player_client.html's generic object system applies the SAME motion-interpolation used for player/bot sprites to every object, fog runs included: when an object's id receives a new x/y, the client does NOT snap -- it glides dispX/dispY from the old position to the new one via Math.round(fromX+(x-fromX)*t) over packetInterval (~41.67ms, matching the sim's ~24Hz tick), unless the jump exceeds SNAP_DISTANCE=48px.
task3_mechanism.hypothesis: config.freeplay.json's visionConeDeg=60 confirms vision is a facing-dependent cone, so both aim AND movement continuously reshape the per-row run list. Because each row's (and each run's) position is interpolated and ROUNDED INDEPENDENTLY, two runs that should sit pixel-adjacent (same row boundary, or column-adjacent within a row) can round to non-adjacent integer positions mid-glide, opening a 1(+)px gap. FogAlpha=160 means fog is a ~37%-brightness dim, not opaque black, over the lit board -- so map layer showing through a gap in the fog layer reads as a LIGHT SEAM against the darker fog, exactly Maxwell's 'negative space lines in the shadows'. This fires whenever runs are actively re-gliding (aim or move) and disappears once interpolation completes (t>=1, exact integer re-alignment) -- consistent with both 'updates every tick when I aim or move' and the original diagnosis's own observation that bars vanish once the transform/position fully converges.
task3_mechanism.why_not_antialiasing: Fog pixels are written via putImageData/putPixel (client ~line 380), an exact per-integer-pixel array write with no antialiasing possible at the fill step. The candidate mechanism is NOT sub-pixel coverage blending -- it's independently-rounded INTEGER positions of adjacent rectangles landing non-adjacent during a glide. This is a client-code-reachable, in-principle-fixable class of bug (e.g. snap fog-run positions instead of interpolating them, or interpolate the whole fog layer as one atomic transform instead of per-run), NOT a GPU/compositor/driver phenomenon.
task3_mechanism.not_yet_established: This is a code-reading-derived hypothesis with a fully plausible, well-evidenced mechanism -- it has NOT been confirmed by directly observing a mid-glide frame where two specific fog runs are provably misaligned. The empirical re-test below did not catch it either.

task_empirical_retest.data: Re-classified the EXISTING N=700 aim-only capture already taken on the byte-verified deployed/swap7-20260830 client (no new capture needed) with classify_light_seam.py.
task_empirical_retest.result: 0/700 raw Stage-1 light-peak candidates -- same null as the dark-dip classifier got on the same data.
task_empirical_retest.interpretation: Does not confirm the mechanism empirically, but also does not refute it: packetInterval (~41.7ms) is much shorter than this capture's achieved cadence (~5fps, ~140-200ms between samples) -- several full interpolation glides complete between consecutive captured frames, so a screenshot-based sampling approach may simply be under-sampling a fast, brief event, independent of which polarity the classifier looks for. This capture also may not have driven enough ACTUAL fog-boundary churn -- the seat spent long stretches of this particular run in open/already-fully-visible areas where few or no fog runs existed to begin with.
